# 2D: AI

## Guide
- [Enemy patrol and chase](./Enemy-Patrol-and-Chase.md)

## Common patterns
Waypoint patrols provide predictable movement; distance tests detect nearby targets; Physics2D raycasts can check line of sight. Add explicit states as behavior grows: Patrol, Chase, Attack, Return, and Stunned are common examples.

## Debugging
Draw the detection ray, show waypoint gizmos, validate layer masks, and ensure AI does not compete with another controller for the same Rigidbody2D. Distance-only detection sees through walls unless you test occlusion.

# 2D: Animation

## Guides
- [Sprite animation and Animator](./Sprite-Animation-and-Animator.md)
- [Sprite flipping and aiming](./Sprite-Flipping-and-Aiming.md)

## Workflow
Import the sheet as Sprite (2D and UI), slice sprites in Sprite Editor, and create animation clips. Use an Animator Controller when states/parameters/transitions are useful; direct sprite assignment may suffice for very simple animations.

## Animator checks
Animator references the correct controller, clips are present in states, transition conditions refer to existing parameters with matching types, looping clips have Loop Time enabled, and no two systems control the same Transform property.

## Sprite consistency
Keep Pixels Per Unit and pivots consistent between frames. Use SpriteRenderer sorting/layers independently of physics layers. Test flipping with child weapons/colliders so visuals and hitboxes remain aligned.

docs.content:
# 2D: Audio

## Guide
- [Audio setup and sound effects](./Audio-Setup-and-Sound-Effects.md)

## AudioSource basics
- AudioClip: imported audio asset.
- AudioSource: playback component.
- AudioListener: usually on the active camera; keep a single active listener.
- AudioMixer: groups sources and controls volume/effects centrally.

For positional 2D effects, Spatial Blend is normally 0. Disable Play On Awake for code-triggered effects. Use PlayOneShot for short overlapping sounds; use looping AudioSources for music/ambience as appropriate.

## Import and performance
Audio import settings trade memory, latency, and CPU use. Choose based on clip duration and target platform. Profile rather than selecting one setting for every sound.

## Troubleshooting
Check source/listener enabled states, assigned clips, source volume, mixer routing/mute, Spatial Blend, pause state, and platform audio settings.

# 2D: Cameras

## Guides
- [Camera follow and pixel-perfect setup](./Camera-Follow-and-Pixel-Perfect.md)
- [Camera bounds and level confinement](./Camera-Bounds.md)
- [Screen shake recipe](../Recipes/Screen-Shake.md)

## Orthographic projection
Orthographic Size is half of the visible vertical world span. Visible width depends on aspect ratio. Set a deliberate camera Z position and ensure the gameplay plane is in front of the camera.

## Follow and confinement
Use LateUpdate for many simple follow cameras, or a camera package such as Cinemachine for richer rigs. Bounds must account for the camera's half-width and half-height. Integrate smoothing and clamping so one does not undo the other.

## Pixel art
Keep PPU/reference resolution consistent and test actual target resolution. Fractional camera positions can create shimmer or uneven pixel movement.

2D Component Inspector Reference
docs.content:
# 2D Component Inspector Reference

Property names can change between Unity releases. This guide explains the purpose of common settings; use the installed Editor's tooltip and version-specific documentation for exact labels.

## SpriteRenderer

| Property | Purpose / when to change it |
|---|---|
| Sprite | Image asset drawn by this renderer. |
| Color | Tints the sprite; alpha can make it transparent. |
| Flip X / Flip Y | Mirrors the rendered sprite without rotating the GameObject. |
| Draw Mode | Simple, Sliced, or Tiled behaviour where supported. |
| Sorting Layer | Broad draw-order category. |
| Order in Layer | Relative draw order inside the sorting layer. |
| Mask Interaction | Controls interaction with Sprite Masks. |
| Material | Shader/material used to render the sprite. |

## Rigidbody2D

| Property | Purpose / caution |
|---|---|
| Body Type | Dynamic, Kinematic, or Static simulation behaviour. |
| Simulated | Whether the body participates in 2D physics. |
| Mass | Affects force response; changing mass does not necessarily change gravity acceleration. |
| Gravity Scale | Multiplies gravity for this body. |
| Linear / Angular Damping | Reduces linear/angular motion over time; labels vary by Unity version. |
| Collision Detection | Discrete is cheaper; Continuous may help fast bodies avoid tunnelling. |
| Interpolate | Smooths rendered movement between physics updates. |
| Constraints | Freeze position or rotation axes when appropriate. |

## Collider2D

| Property | Purpose / caution |
|---|---|
| Is Trigger | Reports overlap events instead of ordinary solid collision response. |
| Material | Physics Material 2D for friction/bounciness. |
| Offset | Moves the collider relative to its object. |
| Size / Radius / Points | Defines collision geometry, depending on shape. |
| Used by Composite | Lets compatible colliders contribute to a Composite Collider 2D. |

## Animator

- **Controller:** state machine asset to evaluate.
- **Avatar:** rig mapping where applicable.
- **Apply Root Motion:** applies animation-authored displacement; coordinate this with scripted movement.
- **Update Mode:** controls evaluation timing.
- **Culling Mode:** determines whether animation is evaluated when not visible.

## Diagnostic order
1. Confirm component enabled and GameObject active.
2. Confirm all serialized references are assigned.
3. Confirm layer and sorting configuration.
4. Confirm physics body type and collider dimensions.
5. Check Console errors and package/version mismatch.
6. Reproduce in a minimal test scene before changing many settings.

Official references: [SpriteRenderer](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/SpriteRenderer.html) · [Rigidbody2D](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Rigidbody2D.html) · [Collider2D](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Collider2D.html)

docs.title: 2D: Components
docs.content:
# 2D: Components

## Common components
- **SpriteRenderer:** draws a sprite. Important fields include Sprite, Color, Flip X/Y, Draw Mode, Mask Interaction, Sorting Layer, and Order in Layer.
- **Rigidbody2D:** controls 2D simulation. Review Body Type, Simulated, Mass, Gravity Scale, Linear/Angular Damping (names vary by version), Collision Detection, Interpolate, and Constraints.
- **Collider2D:** defines a collision shape. Common types: Box, Circle, Capsule, Polygon, Edge, Composite.
- **Animator:** evaluates an Animator Controller and its parameters to select visual states.
- **SortingGroup:** sorts a group of renderers together, useful for multi-sprite characters.

Detailed settings reference: [2D Component Inspector Reference](./Inspector-Reference.md).

## Choosing components
Use the simplest collider that supports the gameplay. Add Rigidbody2D when an object needs physics simulation or relevant collision/trigger interactions. Static level geometry generally does not need to be moved by script.

## Inspector checklist
1. Are references assigned?
2. Is the Rigidbody2D Body Type appropriate?
3. Are colliders enabled and sized correctly?
4. Is Is Trigger set as intended?
5. Do the involved layers interact in the Physics 2D Layer Collision Matrix?
6. Are sorting layer and order correct?

## Common mistakes
A collider alone does not make an object move. Directly changing Transform on a physics body can produce unreliable contacts. A trigger callback can fail due to missing Rigidbody2D setup, disabled objects, or layer filtering.

Official reference: [2D physics components](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/Physics2DReference.html)

docs.title: 2D Coordinate Spaces and Pixels Per Unit
docs.content:
# 2D Coordinate Spaces and Pixels Per Unit

## World space and screen space
World coordinates describe the game scene. Screen coordinates describe pixel positions in the game window. UI coordinates may use a Canvas-specific space. Convert between them explicitly.

```csharp
Vector3 screen = Input.mousePosition;
Vector3 world = Camera.main.ScreenToWorldPoint(
    new Vector3(screen.x, screen.y, -Camera.main.transform.position.z));
```

This example assumes a 2D scene on the XY plane with a camera looking along Z. For production code, cache a camera reference instead of repeatedly using Camera.main, and account for the camera's orientation and desired depth.

## Pixels Per Unit (PPU)
PPU specifies how many source-image pixels represent one world unit. For example, a 32-pixel-wide sprite imported at 32 PPU is approximately one world unit wide before Transform scaling.

Consistency matters more than a particular PPU number. If some assets use 16 PPU and others use 100 PPU, they may appear at very different sizes unless their import settings and Transform scales are planned.

## Pixels and filtering
- **Point:** preserves crisp pixel boundaries, often preferred for pixel art.
- **Bilinear:** smooths texture sampling.
- **Compression:** may reduce memory but can introduce artifacts.
- **Mip Maps:** commonly useful for textures viewed at varying scales; evaluate their suitability for 2D UI and pixel art.

## Camera sizing
An orthographic camera's Size is half the vertical view span in world units. Horizontal span depends on the aspect ratio. Test several window shapes, especially if the game uses a fixed pixel-art resolution.

## Pixel-perfect checklist
1. Consistent PPU across the art set.
2. Point filtering when appropriate.
3. Deliberate reference resolution.
4. Camera movement aligned with the chosen pixel grid if required.
5. Test at target resolutions and aspect ratios.

Reference: [Sprite import settings](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/texture-type-sprite.html)

docs.content:
# Unity Localization and Accessibility Setup

Unity's Localization package supports translated strings, locale-specific assets, Smart Strings for values/plurals, pseudo-localization, and import/export workflows. Package availability and APIs depend on the installed Unity version.

Official Unity 6 manual: https://docs.unity3d.com/6000.0/Documentation/Manual/com.unity.localization.html

## Install and create tables
1. Install the Localization package through Package Manager.
2. Open the Localization Settings workflow and create a Localization Settings asset if prompted.
3. Add the locales your game needs (for example, English and another target language).
4. Create a String Table Collection such as UI.
5. Give entries stable keys such as menu.play, menu.settings, and game.pause.
6. Enter translations per locale instead of hardcoding visible sentences throughout scripts.
7. Add a Localize String Event or LocalizedString binding to UI elements supported by the chosen UI system.
8. For language selection, set the selected locale through the package's documented API and save the user's preference.

Exact menu locations and UI components can vary by package version. Follow the documentation for your installed package.

## Localized assets
The package can provide different assets for different locales. This is useful when art contains text, audio is dubbed, or a region requires a different graphic. Avoid embedding text inside images if it could instead be translated as text.

## Text layout
Translations may be much longer or shorter than the source. Test buttons, subtitles, dialogs, text wrapping, font glyph coverage, and right-to-left layouts if supported. Avoid hardcoded widths that only fit English.

## Accessibility basics
- Provide readable text size and strong contrast.
- Do not rely on color alone to indicate an important state.
- Add captions/subtitles where appropriate.
- Support control remapping where appropriate and give UI focus/navigation clear behavior.
- Test keyboard, controller, touch, and different screen sizes according to the target platform.

## Testing
Use pseudo-localization to reveal clipping early. Test every UI screen with each locale and inspect fallback behavior when an entry/asset is missing. Keep keys stable; change translations independently of code.

Keep runtime state separate from authored data. Use one clear owner for health, movement, pause state, and other shared values.

docs.content:
# Debugging, Testing, and Profiling

## Debugging sequence
1. Read the first Console error; later errors may be consequences.
2. Double-click it to open the source line.
3. Check filename/class name, Inspector references, active scene, and prefab instance.
4. Reproduce in the smallest scene possible.
5. Log state changes rather than every frame.
6. Remove or gate noisy logs after fixing the issue.

    Debug.Log("Reached checkpoint", this);
    Debug.LogWarning("Target has not been assigned.", this);
    Debug.LogError("Required component is missing.", this);

Passing this as context makes Console messages clickable.

## Physics debugging
- Enable Gizmos in Scene view.
- Draw casts with Debug.DrawRay or Debug.DrawLine.
- Verify layer masks, collider sizes/offsets, body type, constraints, and collision matrix.
- Check trigger callback Rigidbody requirements.
- Check whether the collider is on a child while the script checks only the root.

## Profiler
Open Window → Analysis → Profiler. Profile a Development Build on target hardware when possible; Editor overhead changes results. Measure CPU, GPU, memory, garbage collection, rendering, and physics separately.

## Frequent failures
NullReferenceException: missing reference, destroyed object, or initialization-order issue. Missing script: class/file mismatch or deleted/renamed class. Input not detected: wrong map/backend/binding or focus. Physics jitter: Transform writes conflict with Rigidbody simulation. Build-only failure: missing scene, case mismatch, platform API, unsupported package, or Editor-only code.

## Recommended ownership
Gameplay systems own rules/state; UI displays those values. Health should not know HUD layout. Pickups award collection state once, then notify inventory/score. Checkpoints store a position while respawn logic decides how velocity, health, and items are restored.

## Testing checklist
Test repeated triggers, missing references, scene reload, timeScale restoration, checkpoint at world origin, and missing/malformed save files.

docs.content:
# 2D Tilemaps, Sprite Import, and Collision

## Sprite import
Set Texture Type to Sprite (2D and UI). Use Single for one sprite or Multiple for a sheet. Slice multiple sprites in Sprite Editor. Pixels Per Unit determines how many source pixels correspond to one world unit. Filtering and compression depend on art style and target; pixel art commonly uses Point filtering and careful camera/PPU alignment.

## Tilemap workflow
1. Create a 2D Tilemap, usually Rectangular.
2. Create a Tile Palette and drag sprites in to create Tile assets.
3. Separate decorative tiles from solid collision tiles when practical.
4. Add TilemapCollider2D to the collision Tilemap.
5. For large maps, consider CompositeCollider2D to merge adjacent tile boundaries. Configure the TilemapCollider2D composite operation and Rigidbody2D setup according to the installed Unity version.
6. Set the collision Tilemap's layer and verify the Physics 2D collision matrix.

## Collision best practices
- Use composite geometry where it reduces seams and collider overhead.
- Inspect collider outlines in Scene view.
- Check Tile asset Collider Type and TilemapRenderer sorting settings.
- Ensure player Rigidbody2D and collider match the movement controller.
- Keep collision and decorative layers separate if their behavior differs.

## Common problems
- Player falls through: missing/disabled collider, layer matrix, or incompatible body setup.
- Player catches on seams: try a composite collider and tune collider geometry.
- Wrong render order: configure Sorting Layer and Order in Layer.
- Blurry pixel art: check filter mode, PPU, camera scaling, and pixel-perfect setup.
